headline_marked: [[Real game AI]] uses classical search, not LLMs, for speed & accuracy
headline: Real game AI uses classical search, not LLMs, for speed & accuracy
summary: While most AI now means LLMs, this game AI uses minimax and expectimax for provably optimal moves in milliseconds, running entirely in-browser.
details: The AI powering games on lkforge.com doesn't use large language models (LLMs). Instead, it employs classical game-tree search algorithms like minimax, expectimax, and breadth-first search. This deliberate engineering choice ensures opponents are provably correct and respond instantly, unlike the plausible but slower nature of LLMs.

For instance, the tic-tac-toe engine returns a provably-optimal move in approximately 0.3 milliseconds directly on the user's device, with no network calls. This engine has maintained a perfect record, losing 0 out of 1,200 test games.

LLMs, designed to predict the next token of text, are not inherently suited for the deterministic search required in games. While an LLM can fluently discuss game strategy, it may still make a losing move because its objective is text generation, not optimal play.

The engines for tic-tac-toe (minimax + alpha-beta), 2048 (expectimax), and Color Lines (BFS) are textbook examples of deterministic algorithms. They all run in well under a millisecond within a browser tab, offering sub-frame latency.

The 2048 solver, after 250 self-play games, achieved the 2048 tile in 69.6% of games and 4096 in 30%. None reached 8192, indicating the honest ceiling of the expectimax search at approximately 0.5 ms per move.

Tic-tac-toe, being a solved game, is unbeatable by design. The minimax algorithm, with alpha-beta pruning, reduces node exploration by 93% to just 36,528 nodes at the opening move, completing the search in about 0.3 ms.

This approach is not anti-LLM; language models excel at language tasks. However, for games with fixed rules and finite game trees, classical search algorithms remain the most efficient and accurate solution.

headline_marked: [[Humanoid robot ambulance]] developed in Japan for on-the-spot repairs
headline: Humanoid robot ambulance developed in Japan for on-the-spot repairs
summary: GMO Internet Group has launched a specialized van in Tokyo equipped with diagnostic tools, spare parts, and even a replacement robot to fix malfunctioning units.
details: GMO Internet Group has introduced what it calls Japan's first 'humanoid ambulance' in Tokyo. This maintenance van is designed to travel to locations where humanoid robots have broken down, carrying diagnostic equipment, spare parts, and repair tools.

The service aims to minimize disruptions by providing on-the-spot repairs. If a robot cannot be fixed roadside, the ambulance carries a spare humanoid unit that can be swapped in immediately, while the damaged robot is transported back to GMO's repair base.

Currently, only one ambulance is stationed at GMO's Tokyo headquarters. The service is exclusive to humanoid robots deployed by GMO AI & Robotics Trading (GMO AIR) and dispatches are handled on a case-by-case basis.

The exterior and interior of the ambulance were styled by designer Yasumichi Morita, drawing inspiration from emergency vehicles worldwide, featuring purple lightbars and 'Humanoid Ambulance' branding.

This initiative stems from past experiences where damaged robots required lengthy repairs, causing service interruptions. The 'replacement humanoid' concept was developed to ensure continuous operation.

GMO's parent company focuses on internet infrastructure, while its robotics unit resells hardware from manufacturers like Unitree and offers associated services. This ambulance service is positioned as a forward-thinking solution for the growing use of humanoids.

Japan's government has set ambitious goals for its AI Robotics Strategy, aiming for over 30% of the global robot market and a $135 billion domestic industry by 2040. GMO's ambulance service is presented as a proactive measure to gain field-repair experience ahead of widespread humanoid adoption.
